Let’s dive into Chapter 4: Understanding Intersectional Feminism and Privilege.
You know, feminism isn’t a one-size-fits-all movement. Sure, the fight for gender equality matters to everyone, but the way each person experiences oppression—or privilege—depends on so many things: race, sexuality, class, ability, and more. If we really want a movement that lifts everyone up, we have to recognize these differences.
Have you ever been in a conversation about feminism where someone points out that not all women face the same challenges? Maybe for one person, the biggest struggle is dealing with sexism at work, while for someone else, it’s carrying the extra weight of racism, homophobia, or ableism. These parts of our identity aren’t separate—they intersect, and that intersection shapes unique experiences of both privilege and oppression.
Here’s something to pay attention to: privilege is easy to overlook when you’ve always had it. If you’ve never faced discrimination because of your skin color, sexuality, or physical ability, you might not notice how the world is built for your comfort. But for people on the margins, those barriers? They’re impossible to ignore.
Let me share a story. Imagine a group of friends talking about street harassment. Everyone agrees it’s a problem. But then, one friend—she’s a woman of color—mentions that, for her, the harassment comes with racial slurs and unfair assumptions about who she is. Another friend uses a wheelchair, and she points out how inaccessible public spaces turn even basic errands into huge challenges. Suddenly, it’s clear: the fight for equality can’t just reflect the most privileged voices. It has to include everyone’s experiences.
That’s the heart of intersectional feminism. It’s really about listening—genuinely listening—to what others go through. It means accepting that some people have it easier, not because they deserve it more, but simply because the system was set up that way. And if you do have that privilege, you’re in a position to use it to advocate for those who aren’t heard as often, rather than speaking over them.
Most of us don’t realize how much our own internal bias shapes what we believe. Even folks who think of themselves as progressive can get stuck, centering their own experiences and assuming their path is the universal one. Unlearning this habit? It’s a journey. It takes humility, and a lot of openness.
There’s also the challenge of confronting internalized misogyny—the subtle ways we all pick up and repeat harmful ideas about women, sometimes without even noticing. Maybe it’s judging other women for their choices, competing for approval, or ignoring the struggles of people who are different from us.
Unlearning this stuff is uncomfortable. But it’s necessary. It means asking yourself tough questions, being honest about mistakes, and being willing to grow. And here’s the key takeaway: feminism isn’t just about one person’s empowerment—it’s about collective liberation. It’s about making sure we all move forward, together.
